newsitem.title: USA: Many Americans haphazard in approach to saving - study.
newsitem.headline: Many Americans haphazard in approach to saving - study.

text.p: Two out of every three Americans who manage to save money lack any formal strategy for doing so, increasing the chances that they will fall far short of their financial goals, a new survey showed Monday.

The research, released by the Consumer Federation of America and NationsBank, found that the bulk of Americans are trying to save, with 84 percent setting aside some money for retirement, an emergency fund or another major expenditure.
But most still put aside too little, the survey found, largely because of a haphazard approach.

"All of us were a little surprised with the 84 percent who said they were making some effort to save for the future," said Barbara Roper, director of investor protection for the Washington-based Consumer Federation. "That was good news. They're nonetheless falling way behind."
The survey showed that planning itself encourages better savings patterns.

For the one-third of savers who have established a comprehensive financial plan, the survey revealed clear benefits. In households with annual income of less than $100,000, for example, savers who said they had comprehensive financial plans reported saving about twice as much as those without plans.
For households with incomes between $20,000 and $39,999, the median total savings reported by planners was $28,500, twice that of so-called "non-planners."

For those with incomes between $40,000 and $99,999, those with plans said they had saved $89,650, more than twice set aside by others. Households with incomes of $100,000 or more had amassed $325,000 compared with $201,100 by non-planners.

The survey did not specify over what period of time the savings were accumulated. It defined a financial plan as a comprehensive document that includes investment funds, real estate and retirement plans, rather than a simple household budget.

"In the past, we've simply stressed the importance of savings," said Stephen Brobeck, executive director of the Consumer Federation of America. "Now, as a result of our research, we will emphasise that developing a financial plan is the most effective way to achieve savings goals."
The survey was designed to look at links between investment knowledge, attitudes and behaviour rather than to find any correlation between planning and savings levels.
"You can't tell what it is about planning that is so powerful" from the survey results, Roper said.

She speculated that if people take the step of developing a plan, they are likely to make savings a priority and a part of their non-discretionary spending "instead of waiting until the end of the month to see what they have left" to save.

Americans who have a financial plan are also more likely to have saved money for a whole range of goals -- retirement, emergencies, sending children to college, making a down payment on a house, funding a major purchase or helping with the medical expenses of an older relative, the survey showed.
